options: A WHERE condition SQL Server can use an index to satisfy directly, without scanning every row
A query that always returns sorted results
A predicate that only works with numeric columns
A synonym for a correlated subquery
questions.explain: SARGable comes from 'Search ARGument-able' — describing a predicate that's usable as a search argument for an index.

questions.q: Why does WHERE YEAR(SellStartDate) = 2013 fail to use an index on SellStartDate?
options: Wrapping the column in YEAR(...) forces SQL Server to compute that function for every row before comparing, making the index on raw date values useless
YEAR() is not a valid T-SQL function
SellStartDate cannot be indexed at all
2013 is not a valid comparison value
questions.explain: The index stores actual date values, not year-extracted values, so wrapping the column defeats it.

questions.q: What is the SARGable rewrite of a 'was this in 2013?' check?
options: WHERE SellStartDate >= '2013-01-01' AND SellStartDate < '2014-01-01'
WHERE YEAR(SellStartDate) BETWEEN 2013 AND 2013
WHERE CAST(SellStartDate AS VARCHAR) LIKE '2013%'
There is no SARGable way to express this condition
questions.explain: This asks the same logical question but leaves the column itself untouched, letting an index be used directly.

questions.q: What is the common thread among non-SARGable patterns?
options: Anything that transforms the column itself before comparing it — a function call or a leading wildcard
Using any comparison operator other than equals
Combining WHERE with ORDER BY
Using column aliases in the SELECT list
questions.explain: Transforming the comparison value instead (like the date-range rewrite) keeps the column SARGable.

questions.q: Why does a non-SARGable predicate matter more as a table grows?
options: A full table scan is barely noticeable on a small table but can turn a sub-second query into one taking minutes on millions of rows
Non-SARGable predicates only fail on tables larger than 1 million rows
Table size has no effect on SARGability
SARGability only matters for tables without a primary key
questions.explain: The cost of a full scan scales with table size, which is exactly why this pattern is worth catching early.
